title: Drawing and Visual Art Fundamentals
description: Learn to see accurately and draw what you see: line, proportion, form, perspective, value, light, colour and composition, with practice on paper.
audience: A curious adult with little or no drawing training who is willing to practise on paper with a pencil and a sketchbook. Needs school-level proportion and angle; no artistic talent assumed.
outcomes: You'll be able to draw what is in front of you by comparing shapes, angles and proportions rather than naming objects.
You'll be able to make controlled lines and vary their weight on purpose.
You'll be able to construct basic forms and the ellipses that describe circles in space.
You'll be able to place objects in one-point and two-point perspective with a consistent horizon.
You'll be able to simplify a scene into a few values and model a form with light and shadow.
You'll be able to describe and mix colour by hue, value and chroma, and use complements and temperature.
You'll be able to compose a picture with thumbnails and judge your own work against clear criteria.

sources.title: John Ruskin, The Elements of Drawing (1857)
John H. Vanderpoel, The Human Figure (1907)
Leon Battista Alberti, De pictura (On Painting), 1435
sources.licence: Original public domain; modern translations are copyright

Michel-Eugene Chevreul, The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colours (English translation, 1854)
ITU-R Recommendation BT.709: Parameter values for HDTV standards (luma coefficients 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)

modules.title: Seeing and marks
modules.summary: Looking for shapes and proportions, making confident lines, and building forms.

modules.title: Space and perspective
modules.summary: Cues for depth, and the rules of one- and two-point perspective.

modules.title: Light and value
modules.summary: Value as the structure of a picture, and how light models a form.

modules.title: Colour and composition
modules.summary: Describing and combining colour, arranging a picture, and finishing a study.

lessons.title: Seeing shapes, not things
lessons.objective: Look at an object as a set of shapes and spaces, compare lengths and angles by eye, and recognise that perception can mislead.

concepts.title: Drawing from symbols
concepts.summary: When you draw what you know instead of what you see, you draw a symbol, such as an eye as an almond shape.

concepts.title: Shape
concepts.summary: A shape is a flat area with an outline, such as a triangle or an irregular patch.

concepts.title: Negative space
concepts.summary: Negative space is the shape of the empty area around and between objects, and drawing it checks the positive shapes.

concepts.title: Comparative measurement
concepts.summary: Comparing one length or angle to another, instead of judging it in isolation, is more accurate.

concepts.title: Perceptual illusion
concepts.summary: An illusion shows that the eye's impression can differ from measurement, which is why drawing uses comparison.

misconceptions: Believing drawing talent is a gift: drawing accurately is mostly a way of looking, and it can be practised.
Believing you can trust your first impression of length: in the Muller-Lyer figure two equal lines look unequal.
Believing you should start with the details: drawing the large shapes first keeps them in proportion.
sequence: Show a chair drawn from memory beside one drawn by tracing the empty spaces.
Define symbol, shape and negative space.
Show an illusion and measure it: two equal lines that look different.
Teach comparison: ask 'is it longer than it is tall, and by how much?'
Practise: a 10-minute drawing of the spaces around a chair, rated against criteria.
examples: The Muller-Lyer figure: two horizontal lines, each 100 units long, one with arrowheads pointing outward at the ends and one inward; they look unequal and are equal.
A chair's negative space: the shape between the legs and the seat.
A mug seen from the side: height 10 cm, width 8 cm, so it is taller than wide in the ratio 5:4.

figures.shows: Two horizontal lines of exactly equal length, one with outward and one with inward arrowheads.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a ruler across both lines; the figure reports lengths after the learner guesses.

figures.shows: A chair drawn with the negative space shaded.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between seeing the chair and the spaces.

questionPlan.sample: Two horizontal lines are each 100 units long, one with outward arrowheads and one with inward arrowheads. How do their lengths compare?
What is the empty shape between the legs and seat of a chair called?
Spend 10 minutes drawing only the spaces around and between the parts of a chair. Rate how closely the finished drawing matches the chair's proportions.

lessons.title: Line and mark
lessons.objective: Make controlled straight lines and curves from the shoulder, vary line weight on purpose, and tell contour from gesture.

concepts.title: Contour
concepts.summary: A contour line follows the edge of a form, and cross-contour lines wrap around it to show its surface.

concepts.title: Gesture
concepts.summary: A gesture drawing captures the movement and direction of a subject in a few quick lines.

concepts.title: Line weight
concepts.summary: Heavier lines suggest shadow, nearness or emphasis, and lighter lines suggest distance or light.

concepts.title: Ghosting
concepts.summary: Ghosting is moving the pen over the paper without marking, to rehearse the line before drawing it in one confident stroke.

concepts.title: Arm motion
concepts.summary: Long lines come from the shoulder and elbow, because wrist drawing makes short, curved strokes.

misconceptions: Believing a sketchy line shows skill: repeated hesitant strokes show doubt, and one clear line commits to a decision.
Believing line weight is the same everywhere: uniform weight flattens a drawing.
Believing contour drawing means outlining: contour lines also cross the form to show how it turns.
sequence: Show two lines between the same two points: one drawn in a quick, hesitant way and one in a single stroke.
Teach ghosting: rehearse, then draw once.
Show line weight on a simple object: heavier in the shadow side and where objects overlap.
Introduce gesture as speed and direction, not detail.
Practise: twenty straight lines between dots, rated on how straight and how consistent they are.
examples: Two points 15 cm apart: ghost the line three times, draw it once.
A mug outlined at uniform weight versus with heavier lines at the base and overlaps.
A 30-second gesture drawing of a seated figure with five lines.

figures.shows: Two copies of the same simple object, one drawn at uniform weight and one with varied weight.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between them.

figures.shows: A grid of dot pairs for the learner to practise on paper, with a reference line shown after they have drawn.
figures.learnerAction: Print or copy the dot pairs, draw twenty lines, then reveal the reference line to compare.

questionPlan.sample: What kind of line follows the edge of a form?
On a mug, where is a heavier line most useful?
questionPlan.answer: at the base where it meets the table and on the shadow side
choices: at the base where it meets the table and on the shadow side

questionPlan.sample: Draw twenty straight lines between dots 15 cm apart, each in one stroke after ghosting. Rate how many are straight and land on their dots.

lessons.title: Proportion and measuring
lessons.objective: Measure proportions with a pencil and a unit, and scale a drawing up or down while keeping the ratios.

concepts.title: Proportion
concepts.summary: Proportion is the relation between sizes, such as width to height, and it is kept when the ratio is kept.

concepts.title: Sighting
concepts.summary: Sighting holds a pencil at arm's length and compares one length with another, using one of them as the unit.

concepts.title: Scale factor
concepts.summary: Scale factor is the ratio of new size to old, applied to every length.

concepts.title: Grid method
concepts.summary: The grid method draws a grid on the reference and a grid of equal proportions on the paper, and copies the lines square by square.

concepts.title: Head units
concepts.summary: Figure proportions are often counted in heads: teaching canons use about 7.5 or 8 heads for an adult.

misconceptions: Believing you can measure with your eye alone: small errors accumulate, and a unit check catches them.
Scaling only one dimension: to enlarge a drawing, width and height must use the same scale factor.
Moving your arm while sighting: bending the arm changes the unit; hold it straight and lock the elbow.
sequence: Show a drawing that looks wrong, then find the wrong ratio by measurement.
Teach sighting: arm straight, pencil as ruler, mark thumb at the unit and compare.
Compute a scale factor: a 9 cm by 12 cm object drawn 8 cm tall has factor 8/12 and width 6 cm.
Introduce the grid method, with a 2 cm grid enlarged to a 3 cm grid (factor 1.5).
Practise: measure and draw an object using a unit, rated against a photo overlay.
examples: An object 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall has ratio 3:4. Drawn 8 cm tall it is 6 cm wide.
A 2 cm grid enlarged to 3 cm squares has scale factor 1.5: a 10 cm line becomes 15 cm.
A figure 8 heads tall with a 3 cm head is 24 cm tall.

figures.shows: A simple object with a measured unit and a grid overlay.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the unit and grid overlays; the measurements shown are those of the reference, never of the learner's drawing.

figures.shows: A table of heights and widths for objects with a column for the scaled drawing.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the scaled column for a chosen scale factor.

questionPlan.sample: An object is 9 cm wide and 12 cm tall. You draw it 8 cm tall at the same proportions. How wide in cm is the drawing?
A 2 cm reference grid is redrawn as 3 cm squares. How long in cm is a 10 cm line from the reference once redrawn?
A figure is drawn 8 heads tall with a head 3 cm high. How tall in cm is the figure?

lessons.title: Form and ellipses
lessons.objective: Build objects from a sphere, box, cylinder and cone, and draw the ellipse that a circle makes when seen at an angle.

concepts.title: Form
concepts.summary: Form is the three-dimensional volume of an object, as opposed to its flat shape.

concepts.title: Basic forms
concepts.summary: Most objects can be started as a sphere, box, cylinder or cone, adjusted afterward.

concepts.title: Ellipse
concepts.summary: A circle seen at an angle appears as an ellipse, with a long axis (major) and a short axis (minor).

concepts.title: Degree of an ellipse
concepts.summary: The ratio of minor to major axis equals the sine of the angle between line of sight and the circle's plane, so it rounds as you look more directly at it.

concepts.title: Minor axis rule
concepts.summary: The minor axis of the ellipse of a cylinder's end lies along the cylinder's axis.

misconceptions: Drawing the ellipse with pointed ends: ellipses are smooth and rounded at both ends.
Believing the ellipse is flat at the bottom: the near and far edges of the circle are both curves.
Believing the minor axis is horizontal: it follows the axis of the cylinder, wherever it points.
sequence: Start from a coffee cup and ask what shape the rim is from the side and from above.
Define ellipse, major and minor axes, and the relationship to the viewing angle.
Compute: a 10 cm circle seen with the line of sight 30 degrees above its plane has a minor axis of 10 x sin 30 = 5 cm.
Apply the axis rule to a cylinder, a cup and a can.
Practise: draw ten ellipses in a row, widening gradually, and a cylinder from three viewpoints.
examples: 30 degrees: minor axis 5 cm for a 10 cm circle; 45 degrees: 7.07 cm; 90 degrees: 10 cm (a circle).
A can seen from slightly above: the top ellipse is narrower (less open) than the base ellipse, because the base is farther below eye level.
A cylinder lying on its side: its minor axis is horizontal.

figures.shows: Four ellipses of the same major axis (120 units) with minor axes 30, 60, 90 and 120 units, unlabelled.
figures.learnerAction: Match each ellipse to a viewing angle after predicting.

figures.shows: A cylinder with an axis line and two ellipses.
figures.learnerAction: Rotate the cylinder and watch the minor axis stay on the axis.

questionPlan.sample: A 10 cm circle is seen with the line of sight 30 degrees above its plane. How long in cm is the minor axis of its ellipse?
Four ellipses share a major axis of 120 units and have minor axes of 30, 60, 90 and 120 units. Which minor axis shows a circle seen with the line of sight 30 degrees above its plane?
Draw a cylinder from three different viewpoints on paper. Rate whether each ellipse is smooth and whether its minor axis lies along the cylinder's axis.

lessons.title: Cues for depth
lessons.objective: Name the visual cues that make a flat picture look deep and use size, overlap, placement and atmosphere on purpose.

concepts.title: Overlap
concepts.summary: An object that covers part of another appears nearer.

concepts.title: Size and distance
concepts.summary: The apparent size of an object is inversely proportional to its distance, so twice as far looks half the size.

concepts.title: Vertical placement
concepts.summary: On level ground, things farther away sit higher up the picture, nearer the horizon.

concepts.title: Atmospheric perspective
concepts.summary: Distant objects look paler, bluer and lower in contrast because of haze.

concepts.title: Texture gradient
concepts.summary: Repeated texture, such as paving stones, looks finer and closer together with distance.

misconceptions: Believing perspective is only about converging lines: size, overlap and atmosphere give depth without any line construction.
Believing distant objects are always lighter: in haze they lose contrast, and in a dark scene they may be darker.
Believing twice the distance halves the size by area: height halves, and area falls to a quarter.
sequence: Show a flat picture of three trees, with no cues; add overlap; add size; add placement; add atmosphere.
Name each cue in the order added.
Compute: a 2 m figure drawn 4 cm tall at 10 m is 2 cm tall at 20 m.
Explain atmospheric perspective with a mountain range.
Practise: a 4-layer landscape sketch with each layer using at least two cues.
examples: A 2 m figure at 10 m drawn 4 cm tall: at 20 m it is drawn 2 cm tall; at 40 m, 1 cm.
Three hills, each paler and flatter than the one in front.
A cobbled street whose stones shrink as they recede.

figures.shows: A landscape built in layers with each cue toggled on or off.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle cues to see which one produces the most depth.

figures.shows: Drawn height against distance for a fixed figure.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the distance and read the height after estimating.

questionPlan.sample: A 2 m figure at 10 m is drawn 4 cm tall. How tall in cm is the same figure drawn at 20 m?
Distant mountains drawn paler, bluer and lower in contrast illustrate which cue?
Draw a four-layer landscape using overlap and size on each layer. Rate how deep it looks.

lessons.title: One-point perspective
lessons.objective: Place a horizon line and a vanishing point and draw boxes and corridors whose receding lines converge correctly.

concepts.title: Horizon line
concepts.summary: The horizon line is the viewer's eye level, and every object whose eye height matches yours has it pass through its eyes.

concepts.title: Vanishing point
concepts.summary: A vanishing point is where parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to meet, on the horizon line.

concepts.title: Orthogonals
concepts.summary: Orthogonals are the receding lines, drawn toward the vanishing point.

concepts.title: One-point perspective
concepts.summary: In one-point perspective a face of the box is parallel to the picture plane, so its horizontals stay horizontal, its verticals stay vertical and only the depth lines converge.

concepts.title: Above and below the horizon
concepts.summary: A box above the horizon shows its underside, a box below shows its top, and one crossing it shows neither.

misconceptions: Putting the horizon at the top of the picture because that is where the 'sky' begins: the horizon is at your eye level, whatever the sky.
Drawing receding lines parallel: parallel lines in space converge in the picture.
Believing the vanishing point can be anywhere: it lies on the horizon line.
sequence: Stand in a corridor and notice the lines meeting.
Define horizon, vanishing point and orthogonals.
Build a box in six steps: horizon, point, front face, orthogonals, back face, check.
Explain above and below: where the box is relative to eye level decides what you see.
Practise: draw a row of boxes at different heights and a corridor, rated against a checklist.
examples: A standing viewer's eyes are 1.6 m above the floor, so the horizon is at 1.6 m; a person with eyes at 1.6 m has the horizon through their eyes at any distance.
A shelf above the horizon shows its underside, and a table below the horizon shows its top.
A cube in the picture centre with its front face square and its depth lines meeting at the vanishing point.

figures.shows: A one-point perspective scene with three boxes at different heights and a draggable horizon line.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the horizon; before it is released, predict which boxes show tops or undersides.

figures.shows: A corridor with orthogonals shown as faint lines to a vanishing point.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the construction lines.

questionPlan.sample: What is the name of the point on the horizon where receding parallel lines appear to meet?
In a drawing, you can see the underside of a box. Where is the box relative to the horizon line?
Draw a corridor and four boxes in one-point perspective with the horizon at your eye level. Rate whether all receding lines meet at one point on the horizon.

historyNotes: Filippo Brunelleschi is credited with a demonstration of linear perspective in Florence in about 1415 to 1420, and Leon Battista Alberti described the method in De pictura in 1435.

lessons.title: Two-point perspective
lessons.objective: Draw a box turned to the viewer with two vanishing points on the horizon, and say when a third is needed.

concepts.title: Two-point perspective
concepts.summary: In two-point perspective neither face is parallel to the picture plane, so the horizontal edges recede to two points on the horizon while verticals stay vertical.

concepts.title: Direction pairs
concepts.summary: Each vanishing point belongs to one set of parallel edges, so a box has one for its width edges and one for its depth edges.

concepts.title: Three-point perspective
concepts.summary: When you look steeply up or down, the vertical edges also converge to a third vanishing point above or below.

concepts.title: Distance and distortion
concepts.summary: Vanishing points that are close together make extreme foreshortening; further apart looks more natural.

concepts.title: Foreshortening
concepts.summary: Foreshortening is the compression of a form that points toward the viewer.

misconceptions: Believing vertical edges always converge: they do so only in three-point perspective with a tilted view.
Believing any box in two-point perspective has its edges evenly spaced: spacing shrinks toward each vanishing point.
Putting the two vanishing points on different horizontal levels: both lie on the same horizon line.
sequence: Turn a box in one-point and watch the front face stop being parallel.
Introduce two vanishing points and the pairs of edges.
Show the box construction: vertical edge, orthogonals to each point, then the back verticals.
Add the third point for a view looking up at a tower.
Practise: draw a house in two-point perspective with the horizon at eye level.
examples: A cube turned so that no face is parallel to the picture plane has 2 vanishing points for its horizontal edges; its vertical edges stay vertical.
A skyscraper seen from the street looking up has 3 vanishing points.
A set of building windows decreasing in width toward the vanishing point.

figures.shows: A box in two-point perspective with edges coloured by vanishing point.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the vanishing points apart or together and see the box change.

figures.shows: A tall building seen from below with converging verticals.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the third point.

questionPlan.sample: A cube is turned so no face is parallel to the picture plane, viewed level. How many vanishing points do its edges use?
A tall tower is drawn looking steeply up at it, with its horizontal edges also receding. How many vanishing points does the drawing need?
Draw a house in two-point perspective on a horizon at your own eye level. Rate whether both sets of receding edges meet at points on the same horizon line.

lessons.title: Value and the value scale
lessons.objective: Describe the value of an area, simplify a scene into three to five values, and convert colour to grey by luminance.

concepts.title: Value
concepts.summary: Value is how light or dark an area is, separate from its hue.

concepts.title: Value scale
concepts.summary: A value scale is a sequence of equal steps from white to black, often with five or nine steps.

concepts.title: Simplifying values
concepts.summary: A picture reads clearly when its values are grouped into a few masses, such as three to five.

concepts.title: Local value and lighting
concepts.summary: Local value is the object's own lightness; lighting then makes it lighter or darker.

concepts.title: Luminance and grey
concepts.summary: Colour is converted to grey with weights that reflect the eye's sensitivity: roughly 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B for screens (Rec. 709 luma).

misconceptions: Believing colour decides how a picture reads: value carries the structure, and hue is secondary.
Believing equal steps in reflectance look equally spaced: the eye is more sensitive to differences in darks, and scales are designed for even steps.
Believing pure green, red and blue are equally bright: in a grey conversion green is much lighter than red, and blue is darkest.
sequence: Squint at a scene until the details vanish and describe the masses.
Define value and show a nine-step scale.
Simplify a photograph into three values and then five.
Introduce luma weights and compute grey for pure red, green and blue.
Practise: a five-step scale in pencil and a simple object in three values.
examples: A five-step scale from white (100 percent light) to black (0 percent) has steps at 100, 75, 50, 25 and 0 percent.
Pure green (0, 255, 0) converts to 0.7152 x 255 = 182 (of 255); pure red 54; pure blue 18.
A photograph of a tree reduced to three masses: sky, foliage, trunk.

figures.shows: A five-step and nine-step greyscale with a sample colour patch beside them.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the patch along the scale and select the closest step.

figures.shows: The same scene in colour and in simplified three-value form.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between them.

questionPlan.sample: Using grey = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, what is the grey level (nearest whole number out of 255) of pure green (R 0, G 255, B 0)?
Of pure red, pure green and pure blue at full intensity, which appears lightest when converted to grey?
Draw a simple object in three values only. Rate whether the three masses read clearly when you squint.

lessons.title: Light and form
lessons.objective: Model a sphere with the parts of light and shadow, and predict the direction and length of a cast shadow.

concepts.title: Terminator
concepts.summary: The terminator is the line where a form turns from light into shadow.

concepts.title: Core shadow
concepts.summary: The core shadow is the darkest band on the form, just inside the terminator, not at the edge, because reflected light brightens the edge.

concepts.title: Parts of light
concepts.summary: On a lit sphere the parts are the highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, with a cast shadow on the ground.

concepts.title: Cast shadow
concepts.summary: A cast shadow falls opposite the light direction and is darkest near the object.

concepts.title: Shadow length
concepts.summary: For a vertical object of height h in sunlight at elevation angle a, shadow length is h / tan a.

misconceptions: Believing the darkest part of a sphere is its outer edge: reflected light lifts the edge, so the darkest band is the core shadow just inside.
Believing a shadow falls the same way as the light: it falls away from the light.
Believing longer shadows mean a brighter sun: they mean a lower sun, near sunrise or sunset.
sequence: Light a ball with a lamp and name the bands from lit to dark.
Define terminator, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.
Show the direction rule: light from upper left puts the cast shadow to the lower right.
Compute shadow length with the angle: a 2 m post at 45 degrees casts 2 m; at 30 degrees, 3.46 m.
Practise: render a sphere in five values with a cast shadow.
examples: A 2 m post with the sun at 45 degrees elevation: shadow = 2 / tan 45 = 2 m.
The same post at 30 degrees elevation: 2 / tan 30 = 3.46 m; at 60 degrees: 1.15 m.
A sphere lit from upper left: highlight upper left, core shadow lower right, reflected light just inside the lower-right edge.

figures.shows: A sphere with a movable light source and labelled bands appearing after the learner places them.
figures.learnerAction: Place each label before the bands are drawn.

figures.shows: A post and its shadow at different sun angles.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the sun angle and read the shadow length after estimating.

questionPlan.sample: A light shines from the upper left of a sphere. Where does its cast shadow fall on the ground?
questionPlan.answer: lower right, away from the light
choices: lower right, away from the light

questionPlan.sample: A 2 m post stands in sunlight at 30 degrees elevation. How long in metres is its shadow, to two decimals?
Draw a sphere in five values with a cast shadow. Rate whether the core shadow is inside the edge and the reflected light is visible.

lessons.title: Edges and rendering
lessons.objective: Choose hard, soft or lost edges, and build tone with hatching, cross-hatching and graded pencils.

concepts.title: Edge types
concepts.summary: A hard edge is a sharp change in value, a soft edge a gradual one, and a lost edge fades into the background.

concepts.title: Hatching
concepts.summary: Hatching is a set of parallel lines whose spacing and pressure set the tone.

concepts.title: Cross-hatching
concepts.summary: Cross-hatching layers sets of lines at different angles to darken a tone.

concepts.title: Pencil grades
concepts.summary: H pencils are harder and lighter and B pencils softer and darker, with HB in the middle.

concepts.title: Hatching coverage
concepts.summary: Lines of width w at spacing p cover about w/p of the paper.

misconceptions: Believing all edges should be sharp: a mix of hard, soft and lost edges leads the eye and avoids a cut-out look.
Believing darker means pressing harder: more layers or a softer pencil keeps the surface cleaner.
Believing blending with a finger is rendering: it smooths tone but removes texture and edges.
sequence: Show a sphere with all hard edges and one with a mix.
Define the three edge types and where they occur.
Show hatching tones with different spacing and compute coverage.
Layer a second set of lines at an angle: the covered fraction rises from 20 percent to 36 percent.
Practise: a value strip with hatching and one object with a mix of edges.
examples: 0.3 mm lines at 1.5 mm spacing cover 0.3 / 1.5 = 20 percent.
Two perpendicular layers of that hatching leave (1 - 0.2) x (1 - 0.2) = 64 percent uncovered, so 36 percent is covered.
A face with a hard edge at the jaw and a lost edge where the hair meets the dark background.

figures.shows: Three hatching swatches with different spacing and a swatch of cross-hatching.
figures.learnerAction: Order the swatches from lightest to darkest.

figures.shows: A simple still life with each edge labelled hard, soft or lost.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the edge type at each marker.

questionPlan.sample: Lines 0.3 mm wide are drawn 1.5 mm apart. What percentage of the paper do they cover?
Two perpendicular layers of those hatched lines are drawn on top of each other. What percentage of the paper is covered, assuming lines overlap independently?
Which pencil is the softest and darkest?

lessons.title: Colour theory
lessons.objective: Describe a colour by hue, value and chroma, find complements in paint and in light, and use temperature and a limited palette.

concepts.title: Hue, value and chroma
concepts.summary: Hue is the colour family, value its lightness and chroma its purity or intensity (Munsell's three dimensions).

concepts.title: Additive and subtractive mixing
concepts.summary: Light mixes additively from red, green and blue, and pigment subtractively from cyan, magenta and yellow.

concepts.title: Complementary colours
concepts.summary: Complementary colours sit opposite on a wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet in the traditional painter's wheel.

concepts.title: Colour temperature
concepts.summary: Reds, oranges and yellows are warm, blues and greens cool, and temperature is relative to neighbours.

concepts.title: Simultaneous contrast
concepts.summary: A colour looks different next to another: a grey patch looks warmer beside blue, and chroma intensifies next to its complement.

misconceptions: Believing red, yellow and blue are the true primaries of all mixing: they work for traditional paint, while light uses red, green and blue and printers use cyan, magenta and yellow.
Believing colours that are 'the same brightness' have the same hue: value and hue are separate.
Believing warm and cool are fixed: a green leaning yellow is warm beside a blue-green.
sequence: Show a patch and describe it three ways: hue, value, chroma.
Compare three mixing systems with one picture each.
Define complements and compute RGB complements as 255 minus each channel.
Show warm and cool in one landscape and simultaneous contrast with a grey.
Practise: a six-colour limited palette applied to one study.
examples: The RGB complement of (255, 128, 0) is (0, 127, 255); of pure red it is cyan (0, 255, 255).
Traditional wheel complements: red-green, blue-orange, yellow-violet.
Red and green light mixed give yellow; cyan and yellow pigment mixed give green.

figures.shows: A colour wheel with a movable marker showing hue, and sliders for value and chroma.
figures.learnerAction: Move the marker and predict the opposite colour before it is shown.

figures.shows: A grey patch placed on four coloured backgrounds.
figures.learnerAction: Judge the patch on each background.

questionPlan.sample: The colour (255, 128, 0) has a complement found by subtracting each channel from 255. What is the blue channel of the complement?
In the traditional painter's colour wheel, which colour is complementary to blue?
Mix three paint colours from a limited palette and name each by hue, value and chroma. Rate whether your description matches what you see.

historyNotes: Albert Munsell published A Color Notation in 1905, and Michel-Eugene Chevreul described simultaneous contrast in 1839.

lessons.title: Composition
lessons.objective: Plan a picture with thumbnails, place a focal point, and use thirds, leading lines, balance and negative space.

concepts.title: Thumbnail
concepts.summary: A thumbnail is a small, quick sketch used to test arrangements before the final drawing.

concepts.title: Focal point
concepts.summary: The focal point is where the picture is meant to be read first, emphasised by contrast, detail or position.

concepts.title: Rule of thirds
concepts.summary: Dividing the picture into thirds both ways gives four intersections where a focal point often sits (named by John Thomas Smith in 1797).

concepts.title: Leading lines
concepts.summary: Lines in the picture can lead the eye towards the focal point.

concepts.title: Balance
concepts.summary: Balance distributes visual weight so that a large light shape can balance a small dark one.

misconceptions: Treating the rule of thirds as a law: it is a starting point, and good compositions break it deliberately.
Centering everything: a centred focal point is static and uses half the picture.
Skipping thumbnails: the first arrangement that comes to mind is rarely the best.
sequence: Show one subject in six thumbnails with different crops.
Define focal point and the thirds grid and compute coordinates.
Show leading lines and the eye path.
Show balance with weights and negative space.
Practise: six thumbnails of a scene at five minutes each, selected and justified.
examples: A 900 x 600 picture: vertical thirds at x = 300 and 600, horizontal at y = 200 and 400; the upper-left intersection is (300, 200).
A golden-section division of a 1000-unit width: 1000 / 1.618 = 618 and 382.
A road leading from the lower-left corner to a farmhouse at the upper-right intersection.

figures.shows: A 900 by 600 frame with the thirds grid and a draggable focal point.
figures.learnerAction: Place the focal point; the coordinates of the nearest intersection appear only after the learner has estimated them.

figures.shows: Six thumbnail crops of one scene.
figures.learnerAction: Rank them by clarity of focal point.

questionPlan.sample: A picture is 900 units wide and 600 units tall. What is the x coordinate of the left vertical third line?
A width of 1000 units is divided by the golden ratio 1.618 to give the larger part. How large is that part, to the nearest whole number?
Draw six thumbnails of one scene, five minutes each. Rate how different the six are and whether the best one is clear.

historyNotes: John Thomas Smith used the term 'rule of thirds' in Remarks on Rural Scenery in 1797.

lessons.title: A complete study
lessons.objective: Plan and finish a one-hour still-life study in stages, from thumbnails through values to edges, and judge it against criteria.

concepts.title: Process
concepts.summary: A study goes from large to small: placement, shapes and proportions, values, edges, then details.

concepts.title: Time budget
concepts.summary: A fixed time is divided so the large decisions get the most time and the details the least.

concepts.title: Stepping back
concepts.summary: Looking at the drawing from a distance, or in a mirror, shows errors that closeness hides.

concepts.title: Criteria
concepts.summary: A self-review scores proportion, value structure, form, edges, composition and process.

concepts.title: Practice habit
concepts.summary: Short, regular practice with a clear target improves drawing more than occasional long sessions.

misconceptions: Starting with details: finished details in the wrong place must be erased, which wastes effort.
Judging while drawing up close: errors in proportion and value show from a distance.
Believing one good drawing proves the skill: judge a set of studies over weeks.
sequence: Set out the stages with their purposes.
Allot a one-hour budget: 10 percent planning, 20 percent block-in, 40 percent values, 20 percent edges, 10 percent final check.
Show a study at each stage.
Explain how to step back and how to use a mirror or phone photo.
Practise: complete a study and score it against the six criteria.
examples: One hour: 6 min thumbnails and planning, 12 min block-in and measuring, 24 min values, 12 min edges, 6 min check.
A still life of a mug, an apple and a cloth in three values.
Rating: proportion 3, value structure 4, form 3, edges 2, composition 4, process 4.

figures.shows: A one-hour bar with five stages.
figures.learnerAction: Drag boundaries; totals show.

figures.shows: A six-criterion self-review table with 1 to 5 scores.
figures.learnerAction: Score your study.

questionPlan.sample: In a 60-minute study, 20 percent of the time goes to the block-in. How many minutes is that?
Which is the correct order of stages in a study?
Complete a one-hour still-life study and score it 1 to 5 on proportion, value structure, form, edges, composition and process.

courseCheck: A mixed check of: comparing lengths and spotting illusions; line weight and contour; scaling by factor and ratio; the ellipse minor axis; depth cues and size with distance; horizon, vanishing points and counting them for one-, two- and three-point drawing; placing values on a scale and converting colour to grey; shadow direction and length; hatching coverage; complements in paint and in RGB; thirds and golden-section coordinates; and ordering the stages of a study. Practice tasks are self-rated against a short criteria list, and visual-discrimination items use figures built from stated coordinates so the answers are exact.
platformNeeds: A self-rated practice task type: shows a reference image or figure, a timer, a short criteria checklist and a rating control, with an optional 'I did it' log. Nothing is uploaded unless the learner chooses; a learner may photograph their paper to compare side by side with the reference on their own device.

A 'perspective_explorer' figure: draggable horizon line and vanishing points with boxes drawn from them, showing or hiding construction lines. The svg_figure fallbacks in lessons 6 and 7 use fixed drawings.
A 'lighting_explorer' figure: a sphere or cylinder with a movable light that shows terminator, core shadow and cast shadow, and a post-and-shadow view for the shadow-length formula.
A 'colour_explorer' figure: a hue wheel, value and chroma sliders, an RGB complement calculator and a greyscale (luma) converter, plus a swatch-on-background tool for simultaneous contrast.

A 'visual_discrimination' figure type: 2 to 4 images, shapes or strips, from which the learner picks one (longest, darkest, nearer, warmer). All items must be built from stated coordinates or values (svg), so the answer is exact; photographs only from public-domain or openly licensed sources with the licence recorded.
A public-domain image library with provenance (museum open-access collections such as those with CC0 licences) for line, light and composition lessons.
unverified: All external source URLs and licences: the research session had no outbound web access, so none were opened. Gutenberg and archive.org identifiers for Ruskin, Vanderpoel, Bridgman, Alberti, Munsell, Chevreul and Smith are from memory and must be checked; so must the claim that each is public domain in the intended jurisdiction.

Dates: Brunelleschi's perspective demonstration (c. 1415 to 1420), Alberti's De pictura (1435), Smith's Remarks on Rural Scenery (1797), Munsell's A Color Notation (1905), Chevreul (1839) and Ruskin's Elements of Drawing (1857) are from memory.
The rule of thirds being named by John Thomas Smith in 1797 is widely stated but should be checked against the text.
Rec. 709 luma weights are 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722 applied to gamma-encoded RGB; the lesson must say that this is a standard approximation of perceived lightness, not a physical measurement.
The 7.5 and 8 head canons are teaching conventions that differ between sources.
The ellipse relation (minor / major = sin of the angle between line of sight and the plane) is geometry and was checked by calculation, but the writer should draw it with a diagram.
The question about Muller-Lyer lines assumes the figure is built with exactly equal lines (100 units each) in the svg_figure.
Computed by script: sine values, shadow lengths, grey weights, hatching coverage, thirds and golden-section coordinates, and the one-hour split.
